items.prompt: What part of the body sends the smell signal from the nose to the brain?

options.label: The olfactory nerve
options.feedback: Correct. The olfactory nerve carries the signal from the smell receptors in the nose directly to the brain's smell centers.

options.label: The optic nerve
options.feedback: Wrong. The optic nerve carries visual information from the eyes, not smell signals from the nose.

options.label: The auditory nerve
options.feedback: Wrong. The auditory nerve carries hearing signals from the ears, not smell.

options.label: The trigeminal nerve
options.feedback: Wrong. The trigeminal nerve carries touch and pain from the face, including some irritation from strong smells, but it does not carry the smell signal itself.

items.ok_line: It connects the nose to the brain.
items.ko_line: Each sense has its own nerve to the brain.
items.exp_text: The olfactory nerve is the first nerve in the chain that detects smells. It starts at the smell receptors high in the nose and goes straight to the brain, where the signal is interpreted as a smell.

items.prompt: Where exactly in the nose are the smell receptors located?

options.label: On the very tip of the nose, near the nostrils
options.feedback: Wrong. That area is skin and cartilage; the receptors are inside the nasal cavity, not on the outside tip.

options.label: Along the floor of the nasal cavity, near the mouth
options.feedback: Wrong. The floor is mostly for airflow and mucus; smell receptors sit higher up, away from the mouth.

options.label: High up in the nasal cavity, near the base of the brain
options.feedback: Correct. The olfactory epithelium, containing the receptors, lies on the roof of the nasal cavity, just below the brain.

options.label: On the outside of the nasal bones
options.feedback: Wrong. The outside of the nose has no smell receptors; it only has skin and bone.

items.ok_line: Receptors sit near the brain's floor.
items.ko_line: Smell detection is not near the nostrils or mouth.
items.exp_text: The smell receptors are packed into a small patch called the olfactory epithelium, located high inside the nasal cavity. Because it's up there, a gentle sniff draws air upward to reach it.

items.prompt: What does the layer of mucus inside the nose do for smell detection?

options.label: It blocks odour molecules from reaching the receptors
options.feedback: Wrong. Mucus does the opposite: it traps the molecules and helps them dissolve, so they can reach the receptors.

options.label: It dissolves odour molecules so they can reach the receptors
options.feedback: Correct. Odour molecules dissolve in the mucus, which allows them to interact with the receptor cells.

options.label: It warms the air so smells are stronger
options.feedback: Wrong. Mucus mainly moistens and dissolves; it doesn't directly change the strength of a smell by warming air.

options.label: It filters out all odour molecules before they get too far
options.feedback: Wrong. Mucus doesn't filter smells away; it actually helps them get detected.

items.ok_line: It lets molecules touch the receptors.
items.ko_line: It helps detection, not blocks it.
items.exp_text: A thin layer of mucus covers the olfactory epithelium. Odour molecules from the air dissolve into this liquid, and only then can they bind to the receptor proteins on the cilia of the smell cells.

items.prompt: How does a sniff help you smell something faint?

options.label: It cools the air, making molecules lighter
options.feedback: Wrong. Sniffing doesn't cool air or change molecule weight; it moves air faster.

options.label: It mixes the odour with more mucus
options.feedback: Wrong. Sniffing doesn't add mucus; it just pulls more air up.

options.label: It opens the nostrils wider
options.feedback: Wrong. Sniffing does slightly open the nostrils, but that's not the main reason for smelling faint odours.

options.label: It pulls more air upward to where the receptors are
options.feedback: Correct. A quick sniff increases airflow and sends more air—with more odour molecules—to the high olfactory epithelium.

items.ok_line: More air means more molecules to detect.
items.ko_line: Sniffing's job is to move the air, not to cool or moisten it.
items.exp_text: The smell receptors sit high in the nasal cavity, so normal breathing sends only a little air there. A deliberate sniff creates a faster, stronger airflow that carries more odour molecules up to the receptors, making faint smells easier to catch.

items.prompt: Why does a strong smell seem to fade after you've been in the room for a while?

options.label: The smell receptors become less sensitive to that odour
options.feedback: Correct. This is called adaptation: the receptor cells stop responding as strongly to a constant smell.

options.label: The odour molecules are used up by the air
options.feedback: Wrong. The molecules are still there; your nose just stops noticing them as much.

options.label: The mucus layer gets thicker and blocks the molecules
options.feedback: Wrong. Mucus thickness doesn't change like that to block smells.

options.label: The brain forgets the smell after a short time
options.feedback: Wrong. The brain hasn't forgotten; the sensory cells simply reduce their response to a steady stimulus.

items.ok_line: Receptors tire of a constant odour.
items.ko_line: The smell is still there; your nose just adjusts.
items.exp_text: When a smell stays constant, the receptor cells gradually send fewer and fewer signals to the brain. This is a normal process called adaptation, and it helps you notice new smells instead of being overwhelmed by old ones.

items.prompt: What is different about the nerve cells that detect smell compared to most other nerve cells in the body?

options.label: They are the only nerve cells that have no support cells around them
options.feedback: Wrong. Smell nerve cells do have support cells; the unusual thing is something else.

options.label: They are the largest nerve cells in the body
options.feedback: Wrong. Size is not what's unusual; other nerve cells are much larger.

options.label: They can regenerate and be replaced throughout life
options.feedback: Correct. Olfactory neurons are among the few nerve cells that can be replaced when they get damaged or die.

options.label: They never fire signals to the brain
options.feedback: Wrong. They absolutely fire signals to the brain; that's how smell works.

items.ok_line: They can be replaced, unlike most neurons.
items.ko_line: Smell cells do send signals and have support cells.
items.exp_text: Most nerve cells in the body cannot divide or be replaced once they are damaged. Olfactory receptor neurons are an exception—they are continuously replaced from stem cells in the nose. This lets your sense of smell recover from minor damage.

items.prompt: Why can't you smell something that is sealed inside a closed glass jar?

options.label: Because glass absorbs all smell molecules
options.feedback: Wrong. Glass does not absorb smell molecules; it just blocks them from escaping.

options.label: Because no odour molecules can travel through the glass to your nose
options.feedback: Correct. Smell requires molecules to travel through the air; glass is solid and stops them.

options.label: Because the brain cannot detect smells from behind glass
options.feedback: Wrong. The brain detects smells only when molecules reach the nose; the brain has no way to know about the jar's contents.

options.label: Because the glass makes the smell too weak to notice
options.feedback: Wrong. There's no smell at all escaping, not just a weak one.

items.ok_line: No smell molecules get to your nose.
items.ko_line: Glass traps the molecules, not soaks them up.
items.exp_text: For you to smell something, odour molecules must travel from the source through the air and into your nose. A sealed glass jar is impermeable—no molecules can pass through—so your nose receives nothing.

items.prompt: Why do warm foods tend to smell stronger than the same foods cold?

options.label: Warm foods have more smell receptors
options.feedback: Wrong. Receptors are in your nose, not in the food.

options.label: Warm foods produce more mucus in your nose
options.feedback: Wrong. Food temperature doesn't change your nose's mucus production.

options.label: Warm foods are more likely to be eaten quickly
options.feedback: Wrong. Eating speed doesn't change the strength of the smell.

options.label: Heat makes molecules move faster and escape into the air
options.feedback: Correct. Warmth increases the energy of molecules, so more volatile odour molecules leave the food and reach your nose.

items.ok_line: Warmer food gives off more molecules.
items.ko_line: It's about molecule movement, not about your nose.
items.exp_text: Odour molecules are small and evaporate more readily at higher temperatures. Heat adds energy, causing more molecules to become airborne. That's why a hot soup smells more strongly than the same soup cold.

items.prompt: What does the brain do with the signal it receives from the olfactory nerve?

options.label: It interprets the pattern of signals as a specific smell
options.feedback: Correct. The brain compares the pattern of activated receptors with past smells to identify what you're smelling.

options.label: It stores the smell molecules for later use
options.feedback: Wrong. The molecules stay in the nose; the brain only receives nerve signals, not the actual molecules.

options.label: It sends the signal back to the nose to cancel it
options.feedback: Wrong. The brain doesn't send smell signals back; it just processes them.

options.label: It converts the smell into a taste signal
options.feedback: Wrong. Smell and taste are separate senses, though they combine in the brain, but smell doesn't turn into taste.

items.ok_line: It recognizes the pattern of signals.
items.ko_line: The brain processes signals, not molecules.
items.exp_text: When odour molecules bind to different receptor types, each receptor sends its own signal. The brain receives this combined pattern and matches it against memories to tell you what the smell is.

items.prompt: How can the nose tell apart so many different smells if it only has a limited number of receptor types?

options.label: It uses a different receptor for every single smell it can detect
options.feedback: Wrong. There are only a few hundred receptor types, far fewer than the number of possible smells.

options.label: It counts the number of molecules of each type
options.feedback: Wrong. The nose doesn't count molecules; it responds to which receptors are activated and how strongly.

options.label: Each smell activates a unique combination of receptor types
options.feedback: Correct. A single molecule can bind to several receptor types, and different molecules activate different combinations, producing a unique pattern.

options.label: It uses one receptor that changes its shape for each smell
options.feedback: Wrong. Receptors are fixed in shape; they don't morph to fit different molecules.

items.ko_line: There isn't a separate receptor for each possible smell.
items.exp_text: Each odour molecule can bind to several different receptor types, and each receptor type can be activated by many different molecules. The brain reads the combined pattern—which receptors fire and how strongly—to tell apart a vast number of smells from a small set of receptor types.
